content: The document provides a detailed framework for assessing and managing health workforce needs, focusing on various dimensions such as workforce composition, education, training, and regulation. Below is a professional interpretation of the content: 1. Health Workforce Composition and Distribution: The module outlines the size, composition, and distribution of the health workforce, including demographic characteristics, sectoral distribution, and reliance on foreign health workers. Key indicators include health worker density (both nationally and subnationally), distribution by age group, gender representation, facility ownership, and facility type. Migration-related indicators assess the proportion of foreign-born and foreign-trained health workers in the active workforce. 2. Health Workforce Density:g., practicing, professionally active, or licensed health workers). Subnational density is calculated similarly, considering the administrative unit where the health worker is employed. 3. Workforce Distribution by Age and Gender: The percentage of active health workers is analyzed across different age groups (e.g., <25, 25–34, 35–44, etc.) and by gender, providing insights into workforce demographics and potential gaps. 4. Facility Ownership and Type: The distribution of health workers is categorized by the type of facility ownership (public, private not-for-profit, private for-profit) and facility type (e.g., hospitals, long-term care facilities, ambulatory care providers, pharmacies, etc.). 5. Migration Indicators: The share of foreign-born and foreign-trained health workers is assessed to understand the dependency on international labor and training systems. 6. Education and Training: This module addresses the capacity, quality, and gender equality in health workforce education and training, aligning with Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4 on education. Indicators include the existence of a master list of accredited institutions, duration of education and training programs, application-to-place ratios, student-to-educator ratios, dropout rates, and graduation rates. 7. Accreditation and Regulation: Standards for the duration and content of education and training programs are evaluated, including entry requirements, total hours of training, and competencies to be acquired. Accreditation mechanisms for institutions and programs are assessed, including whether they are mandatory and aligned with national health workforce plans. 8. Lifelong Learning: Continuing professional development and in-service training are emphasized as critical components of maintaining workforce competency and addressing evolving healthcare needs. 9. Data Sources and Reporting: Data for these indicators are collected from health workforce registries, facility records, professional councils, labor force surveys, and population censuses. Reporting frequency varies, with some indicators requiring annual updates and others every three years. 10. Purpose and Applications: It also supports international comparability and alignment with global health goals.
